hints: Look closely at the word must. Think about amino acids that are far apart in the chain but end up side by side in the active site. What type of folding brings them together?

Recall what each level means: primary is the sequence, secondary is local coiling and folding, tertiary is the final 3D shape of one polypeptide, quaternary is joining two or more polypeptides. Do all enzymes have more than one polypeptide?
walkthrough:
**Picture what an active site needs**

Think of the active site as a tiny 3D pocket. It is usually made from just a few amino acids that may be far apart in the sequence.

To work, those amino acids must be held in exactly the right 3D position.

**Check primary, secondary and tertiary**

Primary structure gives the correct order of amino acids, so the right R groups are present.

Secondary structure (alpha helices and beta pleated sheets) starts the folding, and tertiary structure folds the single polypeptide into its precise 3D shape. This final folding is what brings distant amino acids together to form the pocket.

**Decide about quaternary**

Quaternary structure means two or more polypeptides joining together. Many enzymes are made of only one polypeptide and still have a perfect active site.

So quaternary can be involved in some enzymes, but it is not a must for forming an active site. That leaves primary, secondary and tertiary as must, which is option B.

options.A: Quaternary is not a must, as many active enzymes have only one polypeptide and so have no quaternary structure.
options.B: Primary provides the correct amino acids, while secondary and tertiary folding bring them into the exact 3D position for the active site. Quaternary is not essential.
options.C: Primary must be involved, because without the correct sequence the correct amino acids would not be in the chain to form the active site.
options.D: Both primary and tertiary must be involved, primary for sequence and tertiary for the final 3D shape of the active site pocket.
